evidence_quotes.quote: This dissertation consists of three essays that explore how changes in water supply quality and/or reliability affect health care expenditures, residential property prices, and residential water charges.

The first essay explores the relationship between episodes of contaminated drinking water and health care expenditures in the United States. The analysis relies on panel data from the 48 contiguous states from 2000 to 2011.

In the second essay, spatial and non-spatial hedonic property price models are used to examine the problem of water supply reliability due to aging infrastructure of public water systems on residential property prices. Water supply unreliability is measured by issuance of boil water notices (BNWs) linked to home sale observations (e.g. number of notices affecting the house prior to the sale).

The third essay examines the impact of access to raw water sources on residential water charges by public service districts (PSDs) in West Virginia. This analysis determines the relative value of raw water from each source. Using regression analysis, we compare residential water charges per 4,500 gallons for PSDs that utilize different raw water sources including the surface water, purchased water, or multiple sources.

Therefore, policies that encourage public water utilities to utilize multiple sources, such as the Source Water Protection (Senate Bill 373) passed by the West Virginia legislature in 2014, may result in higher rates. No statistically significant difference is found between water charges of PSDs that use NRCS’s flood control impoundments and those who use conventional sources. Other factors, such as providing sewer plus water service in the same time result in lower residential water charges.

criterion_notes.c1: Essays 1 and 2 examine drinking water contamination effects on state per capita health care expenditures and public water unreliability capitalization into residential property prices, respectively, rather than water service access as an outcome. However, Essay 3 explicitly examines residential water charges per 4,500 gallons levied by 110 public service districts (PSDs) in rural West Virginia, addressing the tariff/affordability dimension of household drinking-water service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Evaluated under BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: In Essay 1 (full text present, PDF pp. 17-68), SDWA health-based (MCL/TT) violations are used as an environmental proxy for drinking-water contamination to explain state health care spending (under plain C2 this touches regulatory compliance, though Essay 1 still fails C4; under narrow C2 it is a water-quality contamination proxy rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access). In Essay 2 (text present through PDF p. 101), boil water notices (80% driven by pipe breaks/leaks from aging infrastructure) proxy physical water supply unreliability to estimate hedonic house-price capitalization, failing both plain and narrow C2 as a governance-of-access exposure (and failing C4). In Essay 3 (where residential water charge per 4,500 gallons is the dependent variable), the entire chapter (dissertation pp. 136-167, PDF pp. 145-176) is missing due to text truncation at PDF Page 101 (<truncated 162214 bytes>). The Abstract and Section 1.1.3 show a primary focus on physical raw water source types (surface water, purchased water, multiple sources, NRCS flood control impoundments) alongside joint water-plus-sewer utility provision, long-term debt, policy discussion of West Virginia Senate Bill 373 (2014 Source Water Protection law), and a literature section on determinants of water charges citing institutional studies (Bae 2007; Erfanian & Collins 2018). Because Tables 4.3 and 4.5 and Sections 4.1-4.7 are completely truncated, we cannot determine without guessing from the abstract alone whether Essay 3 empirically models any regulatory, institutional, utility-structure, or tariff/cost-recovery rule under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical dissertation across all three essays: Essay 1 estimates non-spatial panel and Spatial Durbin Models on 48 U.S. states (N=576); Essay 2 estimates OLS, spatial lag, and two-stage spatial quantile hedonic regressions on 1,985 home sales; Essay 3 estimates OLS regressions across 110 West Virginia PSDs (Table 4.5).
criterion_notes.c4: Essays 1 and 2 model non-access dependent variables (state per capita health care expenditures in Essay 1; residential property transaction prices ln(P) in Essay 2). However, Essay 3 models residential water charges per 4,500 gallons (Table 4.5), which is a direct household water affordability/tariff outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Population, exposure, outcome, and study design are fully reported for Essay 1 and Essay 2, neither of which is eligible. For Essay 3—the only essay with an eligible water-service affordability outcome—the entire chapter (PDF pp. 145-176, including Sections 4.4-4.6 and Tables 4.3 and 4.5) is cut off by byte truncation at PDF Page 101, so the full set of explanatory variables, exact sample year/construction, and institutional/regulatory specification cannot be verified from the provided text.

study_design: Three-essay quantitative econometric dissertation: Essay 1 state-level panel Spatial Durbin Model (2000-2011); Essay 2 cross-sectional spatial lag hedonic and two-stage spatial quantile regressions (2012-2017); Essay 3 cross-sectional OLS regression of public service districts (full text of Essay 3 truncated)
population_and_sample: Essay 1: 48 contiguous U.S. states from 2000 to 2011 (N = 576 state-years). Essay 2: 1,985 single-family residential property transactions and 350 boil water notices across 22 tax districts in Marion County, West Virginia (2012-2017). Essay 3: 110 public service districts (PSDs) in West Virginia (detailed sample description truncated).
exposure: Essay 1: percentage of state population served by public water systems violating SDWA health-based (MCL or TT) standards. Essay 2: public water supply unreliability measured by boil water notices (count, days, average duration, binary indicator) in the year prior to home sale. Essay 3: access to raw water supply sources (surface water, purchased water, multiple sources, NRCS flood control impoundments) and PSD characteristics including combined water-sewer service, debt, and network length (full set of covariates in Essay 3 truncated).
outcome: Essay 1: annual state-level real per capita Personal Health Care expenditures. Essay 2: log single-family residential property sale price ln(P) and capitalized marginal willingness to pay. Essay 3: residential water charge per 4,500 gallons.
rationale: This 180-page PhD dissertation contains three empirical essays, but the provided text is truncated at PDF Page 101 of 180 (<truncated 162214 bytes>), omitting PDF pages 102-180 (including the entire Essay 3 on PDF pp. 145-176). Essays 1 and 2 are present in the readable text and are clearly ineligible: Essay 1 models state-level per capita health care expenditures as a function of SDWA health-based water quality violations (wrong outcome, failing C4, and contamination proxy rather than a service-access rule), while Essay 2 models residential property sale prices ln(P) as a function of physical water supply unreliability proxied by boil water notices (wrong outcome, failing C4, and physical aging-infrastructure exposure, failing C2). However, Essay 3 empirically models an eligible household affordability outcome—residential water charges per 4,500 gallons across 110 West Virginia public service districts (Table 4.5)—and its Abstract, TOC, and Section 1.1.3 mention raw water sources alongside combined water-and-sewer utility structure, purchased water, NRCS federal impoundments, West Virginia Senate Bill 373 (2014 Source Water Protection law), and institutional water-pricing literature (Section 4.3.2). Because the entire full text of Essay 3 (Sections 4.1-4.7 and Tables 4.1-4.5) is missing due to truncation and eligibility cannot be guessed from the abstract alone, the decision under both narrow and plain Criterion 2 is cannot_tell.
